newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Transport strike hits Belgrade before elections.
newsitem.headline: Transport strike hits Belgrade before elections.

text.p: Striking bus and tram drivers stranded thousands of commuters in Belgrade on Monday morning in a protest over unpaid wages, less than a week before Yugoslavia's federal elections.

"There are only 483 vehicles on the streets today out of 1,009 scheduled," Slobodan Vucenovic, a dispatcher for the Belgrade public transport company, told Reuters. "People are angry, I know. But we managed to cover the busiest lines."
A transport official, who asked not to be named, said the authorities managed to get more trams and trolley-buses running by midday.

Two of six transport unions staged the strike. With federal and local elections in Yugoslavia set for Sunday, a wave of strikes or threatened strikes has hit the country in protest at high taxes and unpaid wages.

State media has virtually ignored strike announcements from taxi drivers, private businessmen and lawyers in an attempt to maintain social peace ahead of the elections in the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro.
Belgrade authorities managed to avert a threatened strike by taxi drivers but lawyers said they had launched a three-day protest on Monday over high taxes.

"Our intention is to block the courts," Radmilo Milunovic of the Belgrade Bar Association, which has about 2,600 members, told Reuters. "Lawlessness and high taxes have brought about 95 percent of my colleaques to the verge of poverty."
The association of private entrepreneurs, which also accuses the government of setting exhorbitant tax rates, said they planned to close their businesses beginning on November 30.
Political analysts say opposition parties hope to capitalise on dissatisfaction among workers. The authorities say the opposition has encouraged strikers.
While crowds waited for hours at bus and trams stops in Belgrade, government-controlled television reported "a smaller number of public transpoort vehicles due to a fuel shortage in the company".
In a city where many people rely on public transport, the strike caused huge traffic jams in the city centre and a lot of employees arrived late to work or not at all.
The drivers' trade union said last week announced it would stage strike unless company management agreed to hold talks on unpaid wages and faulty vehicles.
Belgrade dailies quoted the president of the trade union, Dragoslav Stosic, as saying the drivers' demands were minimal and apolitical.
